Auto-summary (auto): Quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, parameter tuning, and retry/failover strategies. Security questions (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS) surfaced. Agreed to share pricing and a small benchmark harness and schedule POC scoping.
Topics: streaming resumption, idempotency, backoff patterns, param defaults (temperature/max_tokens), KV cache/prefix caching, region failover, console traces, Optimize suggestions.
---
00:00 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, this is Priya and Ethan from our SE team. how's everyone doing?
00:06 Maya: good, thanks; shes excited to get into the streaming part - our use case is in-session personalization so latency is pretty important.
00:12 Samir: yeah we want to understand how streaming behaves under flaky networks and how retries hit cost.
00:18 Priya: cool, we'll show live examples — we'll do a quick API console tour then a small live demo of reconnects and how the SDK surfaces partials and replays.
00:29 Jordan: and we can touch on dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs but focus on hosted since that's the quick path to prod for you.
00:34 Lina: that works. timeline wise we want a small pilot in the next 3 weeks.
00:40 Jordan: perfect, we'll align on next steps at the end.
01:05 Priya: ok jumping into the console, first thing — the streaming endpoint returns deltas incrementally and the SDK exposes a stream object you can attach a resume token to. note: the resume token is not the KV cache — its basically a partial response pointer.
01:22 Samir: so is that the same as an idempotency key? if replay happens do we dedup?
01:28 Priya: good q — idempotency keys are for request-level dedupe for non-streamed calls and retry-safe operations. for streaming we recommend combining a session id + sequence numbers in the client to reconcile partials. the server will accept resume tokens to continue from last sent token when supported.
01:44 Ben: and if the connection drops and we reconnect, do we re-charge tokens twice?
01:49 Priya: there are two layers: transport-level reconnect (which resumes and typically does not re-charge if you use resume tokens), and application-level retries where you reissue the same request — that may count as new tokens depending on whether it's replayed from the model start. our SDK tries to avoid double-billing by preferring resume semantics; if you do a fresh request, you'll often pay for the generation again.
02:10 Maya: hmm ok can you show a live scenario?
02:13 Ethan: sure, i'm going to simulate a broken connection; note: our demo harness uses a small model so cost is minimal.
02:22 [demo session begins — Ethan starts a streaming chat call]
02:30 Ethan: sending prompt: "You are an assistant summarizing product feedback, maximize concision"
02:37 [00:30] AWS-style network flake simulated (connection dropped)
02:45 Ethan: connection dropped, reconnected — we're using resume token 'tok-4392'
02:50 Ethan: you can see the stream picks up at the 3rd chunk, not repeating the whole output — client merges partials.
03:05 Samir: so that saved us about 60% of tokens in this simple case, nice.
03:11 Priya: exactly — and in the console we surface token deltas per request and per-resume. you'll see a small extra window of token overhead for the resumed chunk but much less than a full restart.
03:27 Lina: what's the recommended backoff policy? we've seen exponential backoffs in other APIs but want guidance for real-time UX.
03:33 Priya: for UX we recommend a short fast retry series — e.g., 500ms, 1.5s, 3s — then fall back to a model variant (lower-latency) or to a cached summary if user is idle. avoid infinite retries; also use circuit-breaker heuristics if you hit repeated 5xxs.
03:52 Jordan: we also have pre-built fallback policies in the console under Optimize where you can configure canaries — automatic downgrade to a cheaper model variant on high latency.
04:05 Maya: talk to me about param defaults — temp, top_p, presence penalties — we have quality constraints for legal summaries so hallucination is a big concern.
04:13 Priya: set temperature low (0.0–0.3) for deterministic legal summaries, prefer higher max_tokens only when needed. use presence/ frequency penalties carefully; we also recommend quick evals with a small prompt suite — Optimize can run prompt-level regressions and flag quality drift.
04:31 Samir: do you have examples of prompt sets for decline-reuse or structured output?
04:36 Priya: yes, we'll share a prompt-set template and a small harness for regression testing (I'll attach in follow-up).
04:42 Ben: security questions — does hosted keep logs? how's encryption and KMS handled?
04:48 Jordan: hosted keeps minimal logs for billing and debugging; we provide per-tenant audit logs with redaction options. we're SOC 2 Type II — SAML/SSO is available, and we offer KMS integration for encryption at rest.
04:59 Lina: can you share an SOC2 doc?
05:02 Jordan: yes, will send SOC2 and an example SAML metadata flow plus our KMS whitepaper.
05:10 Maya: good — we have an internal security review so that helps.
05:18 Ethan: switching back to streaming — one gotcha is long-context models and KV cache. we use a KV cache to avoid re-computing earlier attention states; in the hosted setup, prefix caching reduces re-token costs for repeated contexts. sometimes telemetry shows 'KV cash' spelled wrong in automatic transcriptions, ha.
05:37 Samir: sounds like it helps with sessions where user context is stable.
05:41 Priya: yep, prefix/KV cache is valuable for chatty sessions. on Dedicated you can pin KV across GPUs, but on hosted we do a managed cache with eviction heuristics.
05:52 Ben: region failover — what happens if a whole region goes down? do you failover to another region and what about data residency?
05:59 Jordan: policy-based routing: we can failover to another region per your policy, but note cross-region failover may change residency and we log the change. for regulated customers we recommend Dedicated or Private VPC deployments to control residency.
06:15 Maya: any guidance on concurrency and batching to optimize cost?
06:19 Priya: choose batching based on latency SLO; large batched throughput reduces per-token cost but increases tail latency. Optimize provides suggestions based on traces — it will recommend batch sizes and quantization profiles tailored to your token-length distribution.
06:34 Lina: demo the console traces for a request — we want to see latency breakdowns.
06:39 Ethan: sure, here's a sample trace: tokenization 12ms, model forward 84ms, streaming flush 14ms, network 28ms — total 138ms. the console shows token-level cost as well.
06:55 Samir: do you provide per-buffer metrics so we can instrument retries vs application errors?
06:59 Priya: yes, we expose per-route metrics, plus request-level tags. you can set tracing hooks for custom attributes.
07:10 Maya: what about rate limits and quotas for pilot? we need predictable behavior under load.
07:15 Jordan: hosted has rate limits and quota controls per token and per route; we can set soft-limits for pilots and configure burst capacity for short spikes. for production at scale we often recommend Dedicated.
07:28 Ben: any gotchas for idempotency when using websockets vs HTTP streaming?
07:32 Priya: websockets are connection-oriented so resume tokens work well. with HTTP streaming, use chunked transfers and have a session id. idempotency keys are useful for non-streamed calls or if you reissue the same job. also be mindful of sequence numbers to avoid double-applying partial outputs.
07:49 Samir: you mentioned SDK retries earlier — can we turn them off? we want deterministic behavior for debugging.
07:53 Priya: yes toggles in the SDK: auto_resume true/false, max_retries int, backoff_policy name. we'll share defaults; for debugging we recommend setting auto_resume=false and capturing raw chunks.
08:07 Jordan: quick competitor note — some vendors don't support resume tokens or they retry by restarting the whole generation which can double charge. we try to make billing transparent in the console.
08:18 Lina: is there a sandbox or small model we can use for integration tests?
08:22 Jordan: yes the free tier includes small-gen models and a sandbox. we'll give you a sandbox org and credits for the pilot.
08:28 Maya: excellent. last question — how do you instrument hallucination regressions?
08:33 Priya: use prompt-level evals: you store reference outputs and periodically run them via Optimize; it computes diffs against statistical baselines and alerts on drift. we can also run A/B rollouts with canary traffic.
08:46 Samir: ok, that helps.
08:50 Jordan: recap quick: we'll send pricing + SOC2/KMS docs, Priya will send demo notebook + prompt set and the small harness, you (Ben) will share region/egress constraints, and we'll schedule a POC scoping call.
09:05 Maya: sounds good — thanks all.
09:08 Lina: thanks, very helpful.
09:12 Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
